shown_text: How should the evaluator count an imposed half-pot cap (E1-at-most-half: a partner who leaves may take at most half of the pooled assets)? 1. As a renegotiable default, with the bigger contributor's exit cost counted: every pair starts with the cap, either can renegotiate it in the terms; the evaluator credits the anti-domination protection and charges the bigger contributor's exit cost through the stay test. 2. Only if negotiated. 3. Yes regardless: the cap protects.
after_text: Option 1: E1 is a renegotiable default; liberty credits the protection; the bigger contributor's exit cost is charged via the stay test.

shown_text: Read-back: At exit, a lot of times what gets split is physical stuff, not just money: the home, a pet, the furniture, the record collection. Some of it can't be cut in half, and each partner values it differently, often for sentimental reasons. So a fair split is judged by what each person values (by the pleasure it brings them), not by price: each leaves with what they'd call at least their fair share.
in_force_before: Household exit splits a single money pot (E1-at-most-half: at most half of the pooled assets).
after_text: Author: 'yeah' to physical assets, but 'idk if it makes sense to say it as half but also that no one is ever entitled to anything it should be negotiated'.

shown_text: Read-back: No one is ever entitled to anything at exit, money or stuff. What each person leaves with is negotiated between the two. (You weren't sure 'half' even makes sense as the frame.) This revises your earlier pick of the half-pot cap as a renegotiable default.

shown_text: Read-back: When a pair can't agree at exit, the fallback leans on what each person put in and what each values, not entitlement, and not just what each brought or holds.
